title: Principles
author: Ray Dalio
theme: Better decisions come from writing down clear principles, facing reality honestly and testing your thinking against other capable people.
summary: Ray Dalio founded Bridgewater Associates, which grew into one of the world's largest hedge funds. In this book he sets out the rules he and his firm used to make decisions, arguing that anyone can benefit from turning hard-won lessons into explicit principles they can apply again when similar situations return.

The first part tells his own story. Its turning point is an early-1980s market call that he made loudly and got badly wrong, which nearly destroyed his firm. The lesson he drew was humility: instead of asking whether he was right, he began asking how he could know he was right, and he sought out sharp people who disagreed with him.

The second part covers life principles. Dalio urges readers to embrace reality and deal with it, even when it is unpleasant. Painful mistakes, if reflected upon, are the raw material of progress. He describes a five-step loop for getting what you want: set clear goals, identify the problems in the way, diagnose their root causes, design a plan, and carry it through. He also asks people to be radically open-minded and to accept that others are wired differently, so each person should play to their strengths and lean on others for their weaknesses.

The third part applies these ideas to organisations. Dalio wants an idea meritocracy, where the best ideas win rather than the most senior voice. That depends on radical truthfulness and radical transparency: people say what they really think, mistakes are surfaced openly, and meetings are often recorded. Opinions are weighted by each person's believability, based on their track record. He treats the organisation as a machine made of culture and people, which managers must constantly observe, diagnose and improve.
The book's message is that disciplined reflection, honesty and principled decision-making compound over time.
takeaway: Turn your mistakes into written principles, seek out thoughtful disagreement, and weigh opinions by proven believability.

questions.q: What does Dalio mean by a 'principle'?
options: A legal rule set by regulators
A fundamental truth or rule that guides action in recurring situations
A one-off decision made under pressure
A company's financial target for the year
questions.why: Principles are reusable ways of handling situations that come up again and again.

questions.q: What early setback reshaped Dalio's thinking?
options: Losing a court case against a client
Being fired from his first job
A confident but wrong market prediction that nearly ruined his firm
A failed attempt to start a technology company
questions.why: The costly wrong call in the early 1980s taught him humility and the value of testing his views.

questions.q: After that setback, which question did Dalio learn to ask?
options: How do I know I'm right?
Who is to blame?
How can I avoid all risk?
What do most people believe?
questions.why: He shifted from defending his views to testing them against capable people who disagreed.

questions.q: How does Dalio view painful mistakes?
options: As signs of personal failure to be hidden
As bad luck that teaches nothing
As problems best handled by someone else
As sources of progress when followed by reflection
questions.why: He argues that pain combined with reflection leads to learning and improvement.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of Dalio's five-step process?
options: Plan, act, review, reward, repeat
Goals, problems, diagnosis, design, doing
Diagnose, set goals, act, design, review
Research, debate, vote, act, report
questions.why: He moves from clear goals to spotting problems, finding root causes, designing a plan and executing it.

options: A system where the most senior person decides
A system where every vote counts equally
A system where the best ideas win regardless of who proposes them
A system where ideas are judged by their popularity
questions.why: Dalio wants decisions driven by the quality of reasoning, not rank or headcount.

questions.q: In 'believability-weighted' decision-making, whose views count most?
options: People with strong records of success in the relevant area
The loudest people in the room
The newest employees
Outside consultants
questions.why: Opinions are weighted by demonstrated competence and track record on the matter at hand.

questions.q: What does 'radical transparency' involve at Bridgewater?
options: Publishing all trading positions to the public
Sharing salaries with competitors
Keeping criticism strictly private
Openly surfacing mistakes and honest views, often with meetings recorded
questions.why: Open information and candour let problems be seen and fixed quickly.

questions.q: Why does Dalio stress that people are 'wired differently'?
options: So that managers can ignore weaknesses entirely
So that people use their strengths and rely on others where they are weak
To justify hiring only one personality type
To argue that training is useless
questions.why: Knowing how people differ lets teams match roles to strengths and cover weaknesses.

questions.q: How does Dalio describe an organisation?
options: As a family that should avoid conflict
As a market with no central design
As a machine made of culture and people that managers keep improving
As a hierarchy where orders flow one way
questions.why: He asks managers to compare outcomes with goals and redesign the machine when it falls short.
